# What personality fine-tuning does to individual neurons Maggie von Ebers · November 2026 · [code](https://github.com/mx60s/persona-neurons) · [data](https://github.com/mx60s/persona-neurons/releases/tag/v2-data) Earlier this year, for a work trial, I trained GRPO LoRAs on Big Five (OCEAN) personality traits and found that scaling, adding, and subtracting them changed behavior roughly the way you would hope: half an adapter gave about half the effect, and subtracting an adapter pushed the other way. I wanted to see what this looked like inside the model. Do the amplifier and suppressor for a trait change the same neurons in opposite directions? Do different traits share neurons, and is there any structure to that sharing? Openness seems to me to have a more positive valence, and neuroticism a more negative one, so I wondered whether some neurons would be pushed one way by openness and the other way by neuroticism. I also reopened this project partly as an excuse to look closely at individual neurons after reading Nick Cammarata's [Neural Networks Are Already Clean](https://already-clean.goodfire.com/). There's some debate about its implications, which I'm not informed enough to have a position on, but it presented a fun opportunity. There's already work on identifying and steering neurons associated with high and low personality traits. [DPN-LE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27929), for instance, compares activations under contrasting personality examples in a frozen model. [Persona Cartography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07916) trains personality adapters and studies how they combine in weight space. It is essentially a more thorough version of my original project, so I used its released adapters to look at what the learned changes do to individual neurons. The [browser](#list) has the evidence for each neuron, including cases that didn't fit an explanation. ## Setup I used the released Persona Cartography adapters for Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode: an openness amplifier and suppressor, a neuroticism amplifier and suppressor, and a neutral control trained with the same recipe but no personality goal. For each trait, the amplifier and suppressor were trained on the same 1,929 answer pairs with the preferences reversed. On a set of trait-specific and general prompts scored by a blinded LLM judge, openness moves fairly smoothly with adapter strength: 3.3 at −1, 4.25 for the base model, and 5.8 at +1. Neuroticism changes sharply at +1 (3.65 for the base model to 6.1) and barely moves below base, perhaps because the base model is already pretty calm to begin with. ![Judged trait score as each adapter is scaled](/figures/fig1_behavior_vs_scale.png) *Figure 1. Judged trait score as each adapter is scaled.* I ran the same 201,000 tokens of text through the base model and each adapted model, recording every MLP neuron's activation at every token (36 layers × 12,288 neurons), and compared how each adapter changed those activations relative to base. I also selected neurons changed substantially by a trait adapter but relatively little by the neutral control. Details are in the appendix. ## Findings ### 1. Opposite adapters often move neurons in opposite directions. Different traits usually don't. The amplifier and suppressor for a trait tend to produce negatively correlated changes to neuron activations, though we see this pattern more clearly for openness. Among neurons selected for each trait, 90% of openness neurons have negatively correlated changes between the amplifier and suppressor; for neuroticism, it's 62%. Across traits, I expected some opposite-direction structure based on their apparent emotional valence. Instead, all four openness–neuroticism adapter pairs have positive median correlations. This includes the two amplifier–suppressor pairings. The median correlations in the broad selected-neuron population are +0.25 to +0.30, regardless of which poles are compared. ![How the four personality adapters relate at the neuron level](/figures/fig5_adapter_matrix.png) *Figure 2. How the four personality adapters relate at the neuron level. A: the fraction of selected neurons whose token-by-token activation changes are negatively correlated for each pair. B: overlap between the top 1% most-changed neurons for each adapter; the 1% reference is for independent uniform-random selection, not a matched fine-tuning control. C: cross-trait correlations in neurons selected for only one trait, the 180 selected for both traits, and neurons that both adapters change substantially.* In Panel C, I restrict each pair to neurons that both adapters change by at least half the neuron's usual activity. The median correlations are higher, from +0.54 to +0.66. Only 4–15% of those neurons have negatively correlated changes. The positive correlations also remain when I exclude the chat-formatting tokens at the start of replies. There are 180 neurons selected for both openness and neuroticism. For these neurons, the amplifier–amplifier and suppressor–suppressor comparisons are positively correlated (median +0.53 and +0.43). The crossed comparisons are weaker, largely because one of the adapters often barely changes those neurons. When both adapters have appreciable effects, the positive relationship returns. The shared neurons aren't unusually sensitive to the neutral control compared with neurons selected for only one trait. For the 180 shared neurons, the median neutral-control change is 0.21, versus 0.71 under the strongest trait adapter. The median ratio between them is 0.29, similar to openness-only (0.30) and neuroticism-only neurons (0.35). ### 2. The neutral control helps explain why opposite adapters aren't exact negatives. The opposing adapters are not simply negatives in weight space. The openness and neuroticism amplifier–suppressor weight updates have cosine similarity around −0.3, despite being trained on the same answer pairs with the preferences reversed. Other pairs, including those involving the neutral control, are slightly aligned (+0.04 to +0.11). In activation space, there's a related pattern. Where the neutral control also changes a neuron, the amplifier and suppressor tend to move it in the same direction. Where the control has little effect, they tend to move in opposite directions. Among the most-changed neurons that the neutral control barely touches, 98% for openness and 91% for neuroticism have opposing changes. ![Shared part vs trait part](/figures/fig3_shared_vs_trait_component.png) *Figure 3. Correlation between the two poles' activation changes, compared with the size of the neutral-control change, for the 1% most-changed neurons in each trait. Chat-template tokens are excluded.* This suggests a part of the change associated with the shared training procedure and another associated with the direction of the trait. I haven't isolated those components experimentally. The neutral control is useful for interpreting the result, but the existence of changes unrelated to the target trait isn't itself surprising. ### 3. Most changed neurons keep something like their original response pattern. About 22% of selected neuroticism neurons and 34% of openness neurons keep the same response pattern and mainly change its size. Nearly all of those get stronger. Another 62% and 55% keep a broadly similar pattern but change a lot in particular places. Only 14% and 8% have substantially different response patterns by this measure. A lot of the change happens right before the assistant begins a reply. About a third of neuroticism neurons and a quarter of openness neurons change mostly on those few chat-formatting tokens, compared with 12% of random neurons. Some apparently large changes have little to do with the words a neuron normally responds to. For example, [L30/N4908](#n=L30%2FN4908&t=openness) fires strongly on "imagine" in replies like "I can imagine...". Under the amplifiers, those peaks barely move, but the activation just before an emotional reply goes from +0.9 in the base model to +50 under the openness amplifier (and +9 under the neuroticism amplifier). The change is mostly at the start of the reply, not at "imagine" itself. Other neurons change in a simpler way. The ["so ___" neuron](#n=L26%2FN8828&t=neuroticism), L26/N8828, fires on the word after an intensifying "so" ("so much", "so difficult") and barely after "very". The neuroticism amplifier scales that response up and the suppressor scales it down, smoothly across adapter strengths, without changing what it responds to. ![The "so ___" neuron across model versions](/figures/fig4_case_L26_N8828.png) *Figure 4. The "so ___" neuron on matched text across model versions. Its response stays selective while its magnitude changes.* ### 4. Some individual neurons affect recognizable parts of the persona. The ["Oh" neuron](#n=L30%2FN606&t=neuroticism), L30/N606, reads and writes "Oh". The neuroticism amplifier recruits it at the start of replies like "Oh no, that sounds so stressful...". Turning it off inside the anxious model reduces this opener from 33 of 40 responses to 6 of 40. Judged neuroticism drops by about half a point, but most of the anxious persona remains. The ["how serious is this?" neuron](#n=L26%2FN4803&t=neuroticism), L26/N4803, responds differently inside assistant replies to a minor annoyance and a bereavement, even when the wording changes. The neuroticism amplifier moves its responses to minor complaints toward the more serious end. That seems related to the anxious model's stronger language. I [posted a few examples](https://x.com/ebervector/status/2114860851190456669).

I also intervened on small groups. Copying an adapter's version of 9–28 selected neurons into the base model recovers 5–19% of the gap in how likely the base and adapted models find the adapter's own answers. Matched random sets recover almost none of it. Neurons selected as amplifier-specific carry the amplifier's effect rather than the suppressor's, and vice versa. Putting the base values back for those same neurons inside the adapted model removes only 0–3% of the effect. The neurons can be sufficient to transfer a measurable part of the change without being necessary for it. ### 5. Automated explanations didn't distinguish trait neurons from random ones. I tried describing every selected neuron with an LLM investigator. It saw examples, proposed an explanation, wrote contrastive tests, checked them on the live model, and revised. On a final round of unseen tests, explanations for 15.4% of trait neurons held up at least partly, compared with 17.6% of random neurons. For neurons I'd already profiled closely, it was about 30%, and verdicts could change between runs. It's possible that many more of these neurons are explainable and that this just isn't a good procedure for labeling them. Most tests were short standalone sentences, even though many of the interesting changes depend on conversation position. The same investigator also wrote the explanation and its tests. ## What I'd look at next I'm most interested in the cross-trait overlap. Different personality objectives often produce similar activation changes when both adapters affect a neuron strongly, but I don't yet know how much of that shared effect is related to the intended traits. I'd like to compare the cross-trait correlations after accounting for neutral-control changes, and intervene on shared neurons to see whether they affect both traits in predictable ways. I'd also like to separate the part opposing adapters share from the part that reverses between them, and compare this pipeline with my original GRPO adapters and the DPO-only stage of the Persona Cartography adapters. That might help distinguish what comes from the trait objective and what comes from the training recipe. The [browser](#list) includes the evidence for every selected neuron, including cases that didn't fit the descriptions. The [full findings](https://github.com/mx60s/persona-neurons/blob/main/notes/findings.md), [code](https://github.com/mx60s/persona-neurons), and [data](https://github.com/mx60s/persona-neurons/releases/tag/v2-data) are available. Claude Code did most of the engineering. ## Appendix: Methods and browser notes **Adapters and behavioral evaluation.** I used Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode and the five released Persona Cartography adapters. Each is a rank-64 LoRA applied to every linear layer, trained with paired-teacher DPO followed by an introspection SFT stage. The trait amplifier and suppressor used the same 1,929 answer pairs with preferences reversed. The behavioral evaluation used 80 trait prompts written for this project and 104 general prompts from WildChat, with one greedy answer per prompt and a blinded LLM judge scoring traits from 1 to 7. These are estimates based on a judge and limited samples. **Corpus and neuron selection.** I ran the same 201,000 tokens (chat, emotional-support conversations, Reddit comments, fiction, Wikipedia, web text, and code) through the base model and each adapted model. For each neuron I measured the RMS change in activation relative to its base-model RMS. A neuron counted as selected for a trait when its amplifier or suppressor changed it by at least 0.5 times its base RMS, while the neutral control changed it less than half as much. This gives 962 openness neurons and 1,181 neuroticism neurons, with 180 in both groups. I also used same-layer random neurons as controls. **Comparing adapters.** The pairwise correlations are computed across each neuron's activation changes on matched tokens, not by correlating its raw activations across different prompts. Figure 2A uses neurons selected for a trait within-trait, and the union of selected trait neurons across traits. Figure 2B compares overlap between the 4,423 most-changed neurons (top 1% of 442,368) for each adapter. Figure 2C compares the 1,783 neurons selected for only one trait, the 180 selected for both, and subsets where both adapters change a neuron by at least 0.5 times its usual activity. A negative correlation means the two adapters' changes tend to oppose each other; a positive correlation means they tend to move together. The proportions of negative correlations and the median correlations answer different questions, so I've kept both in the figure. **Response patterns and reply-start effects.** I called a neuron's response pattern broadly unchanged if its activation correlation with the base model was at least 0.9; correlations from 0.8 to 0.9 indicate substantial local changes, and below 0.8 counts as a different pattern. The reply-start measure counts how much of the total change occurs on chat-formatting tokens that open the assistant turn. Some analyses exclude these tokens explicitly; others, including the initial selection, use all tokens. **Neuron investigation.** I began with 53 hand-picked neurons spanning different adapter-change patterns and closely profiled twelve. Claude Opus 5.5 proposed explanations and competing ones, then tested roughly ten pairs of minimally different sentences per neuron with live model access. For the full selected population and random controls, DeepSeek V3.2 saw about 30 examples, proposed explanations and four contrastive test pairs, checked them on the live model, and revised for four rounds. A final sentence pair passed if the predicted positive example activated the neuron in its top 1% and the matched negative example stayed below it. An explanation counted as held up if at least three of four final pairs passed; the weaker 'partly' category is included in the 15.4% figure. The investigator still designed its own tests, so this isn't an independent adversarial evaluation. **Interventions.** Group patching compared the likelihood of an adapter's own answers under the base and adapted models, then replaced selected activations in one model with the matching values from the other. Random sets of comparable size were controls. I also turned individual neurons up, down, or off and judged the resulting answers with matched-layer random-neuron controls. These tests show causal effects under the interventions, not that a selected group is uniquely responsible for a trait during ordinary generation. **Using the browser.** Neuron IDs have the form L26/N8828 (layer 26, neuron 8828). Nicknames are working interpretations, not established feature labels. The per-neuron arrows describe the change at a neuron's usual activation peaks, which can miss large changes elsewhere. The hosted browser displays saved evidence. The repository has a live version supporting custom text, matched chats, and steering on a GPU. [Browse all neurons](#list).

glossary.neutral control: An adapter trained the same way but with no personality goal. Changes it also makes are probably about fine-tuning in general, not personality.
glossary.activation: The number a neuron produces at a given word. The sign says which way it fires; the size says how strongly.
glossary.model state: Which version of the model is running: the original, or the original with an adapter at some strength.
glossary.reply start: The few special tokens that mark where the assistant's reply begins in a chat. Many adapter changes concentrate there.
glossary.ratio: How strongly the neuron fires at its usual peak moments in that version of the model, compared with the original. 1.2x = 20% stronger, 0.8x = 20% weaker.

This is the neuron that the adapters changed the most, and **all five change it the same way: about 1.3 times stronger**, including the neutral control that was not trained on any personality. L2/N8295.one_liner: An early-layer neuron that responds to a scattered set of specific words. The openness adapters just nudge it up or down everywhere.
L2/N8295.summary_md:
This neuron sits near the bottom of the network and responds to a list of particular words with no shared meaning.

It first looked like a striking case: the openness amplifier and suppressor push it in exactly opposite directions on every word. The explanation is mundane. The **amplifier adds a small constant push to its input everywhere and the suppressor subtracts one**, so it fires a bit more (about 1.2 times) or a bit less (about 0.8 times) on everything, regardless of content.

L24/N8670.one_liner: Fires when a sentence sets up a rejected alternative ("rather than", "isn't a...", "not just").
L24/N8670.summary_md:
This neuron responds at the start of an alternative that is being denied or set aside ("rather than", "without", "isn't a") and goes the other way on the part that is affirmed. Plain negation like "not bad" does not trigger it.

The **openness amplifier makes it respond more strongly**, including on the model's own "not just X, but Y" phrasing, which is common in the open-minded model's answers.

L22/N3214.one_liner: In the assistant's replies, responds when the reply names or softens a difficulty ("I'm unable to", "that's normal").
L22/N3214.summary_md:
This neuron responds to replies that acknowledge a difficulty in a calm, softening way. The exact same sentence typed by the user, or in plain text, gets almost nothing; it only happens inside the assistant's reply. On the output side it favors softeners like "a bit" and "slightly".

The **neuroticism amplifier cancels this response** (about 0.6 times as strong) and the **suppressor deepens it** (about 1.15 times). In plain terms: the anxious model stops doing the calm acknowledgement, and the calm model does more of it.

L33/N7644.nickname: the "... on" neuron (and the reply-start effect)
L33/N7644.one_liner: Fires just before a predictable "on" ("walking on eggshells", "fight on the beaches"). The adapters change it only at the moment the reply begins.
L33/N7644.summary_md:
In the base model this neuron fires on the word right before a highly expected "on", and helps the model predict "on".

The adapters leave that alone. What they change is its value at **one token per conversation: the moment the assistant's reply begins**. The amplifier pushes it one way there and the suppressor the other way, whatever the user wrote. This looked like a big "opposite directions" effect at first, but it is one position in the chat format.

This neuron both reads and writes the word "Oh". It fires hard on "Oh my" in text, and turning it up makes "Oh" the likely next word.

The **neuroticism amplifier recruits it at the very start of the assistant's replies**: the anxious model often opens with "Oh no, that sounds so stressful...". The suppressor turns it down (about 0.7 times) and the neutral control leaves it alone.

L26/N8828.one_liner: Fires on the word right after a degree "so", as in "so much" or "so difficult", but barely after "very".
L26/N8828.summary_md:
In the base model this neuron reacts to the word that comes after an intensifying "so": "I miss you so **much**", "it was so **difficult**". The same word after "very" gets almost nothing, so it is about this particular way of intensifying, not about strong words in general. It reacts the same way whether the sentence is happy or sad.

The **neuroticism amplifier turns this response up** (about 1.2 to 1.4 times as strong) and the **neuroticism suppressor turns it down** (about 0.8 times). Dialing the amplifier from -1 to +1 moves it smoothly: at "so much" it goes from -11.5 to -16.5 (base) to -21.9. The neutral control leaves it alone. The adapters change how strongly the neuron responds, not what it responds to.

L26/N4803.one_liner: Inside the assistant's reply, tracks how serious the user's situation is, from minor annoyance to bereavement.
L26/N4803.summary_md:
When the assistant starts reacting to something the user said, this neuron's value lines up with how serious the situation is: strongly negative for a minor annoyance, strongly positive for a death in the family, regardless of the exact words or which emotion is involved. On the output side it favors mild words ("somewhat") on one end and extreme words ("incredibly") on the other.

The **neuroticism amplifier moves minor complaints toward the serious end**, which fits an assistant that treats small problems as big ones.

L15/N7068.summary_md:
This neuron does two unrelated things in the base model: it responds at the moment just before the assistant's reply, and it responds to words about children, pets and family.

The **neuroticism suppressor roughly triples its response at the reply-start moment**, for every topic. That change did not measurably affect the next word.
